Aceclofenac: A glycolic acid ester of diclofenac developed in Spain; widely used in Europe and India for osteoarthritis, RA and ankylosing spondylitis. First approval/introduction: Patented 1983; approved 1992 (Prodesfarma / Almirall, Spain). Tramadol Hydrochloride: A synthetic codeine analogue; brought under India's NDPS Act as a psychotropic substance in 2018 due to misuse. First approval/introduction: Patented 1972; launched 1977 in West Germany (Grünenthal GmbH); US FDA 1995. Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): On the WHO List of Essential Medicines and the most widely used analgesic–antipyretic worldwide; onset ~37 minutes after an oral dose. First approval/introduction: Synthesised 1877 (Harmon Northrop Morse); clinical use from 1887; widely marketed from 1950s.
Aceclofenac 100 mg + Tramadol 37.5 mg + Paracetamol 325 mg
Multimodal analgesia: peripheral anti-inflammatory (aceclofenac), central non-opioid (paracetamol) and weak opioid/monoaminergic (tramadol) mechanisms.

Aceclofenac Inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (preferential COX-2) reducing prostaglandin synthesis; also inhibits IL-1 and TNF and stimulates cartilage matrix synthesis. Analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic. Receptor / target profile: Inhibits COX (preferential COX-2) and suppresses IL-1beta and TNF; stimulates glycosaminoglycan synthesis in cartilage.

Tramadol Hydrochloride Weak mu-opioid agonist (mainly via active metabolite O-desmethyltramadol, formed by CYP2D6) plus inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake. Receptor / target profile: Racemate: (+)-enantiomer and M1 are mu-opioid agonists (M1 ~6x more potent); (+)-tramadol inhibits serotonin and (−)-tramadol norepinephrine reuptake.

Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis centrally (COX in CNS), modulates descending serotonergic pathways and acts on the hypothalamic heat-regulating centre; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory action. Receptor / target profile: Central COX inhibition (peroxidase site) and actions of metabolite AM404 on TRPV1 and endocannabinoid systems; weak peripheral anti-inflammatory activity.
Hepatic – CYP2C9 to 4'-hydroxyaceclofenac (main), small amounts of diclofenac
Summary: Rapid, complete absorption; Tmax 1.25–3 h. >99% protein bound. Metabolised to 4'-hydroxyaceclofenac and diclofenac (CYP2C9). Half-life ~4 h.
Hepatic – CYP2D6 (O-desmethyltramadol, M1, active) and CYP3A4 (N-demethylation); glucuronidation
Summary: Bioavailability ~75%; Tmax ~2 h. Metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4. Half-life ~6 h (metabolite ~7 h). Renally excreted.
Hepatic – glucuronidation, sulfation; ~5–10% CYP2E1 to NAPQI
Summary: Rapidly absorbed; Tmax 0.5–1 h. Glucuronidated and sulfated; small fraction via CYP2E1 to toxic NAPQI (detoxified by glutathione). Half-life 1–3 h.

Aceclofenac: Take after food or with milk; avoid alcohol (GI bleeding).
Tramadol Hydrochloride: With or without food; no alcohol.
Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): With or without food; avoid alcohol.
Aceclofenac: BP, renal function, LFTs and CBC on prolonged use; signs of GI bleeding.
Tramadol Hydrochloride: Respiratory status; sedation; misuse; sodium; glucose.
Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): LFTs if high doses long-term or risk factors.

Aceclofenac: Nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, GI bleeding, renal failure, convulsions (rare). Supportive care; activated charcoal. Tramadol Hydrochloride: Miosis, vomiting, respiratory depression, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse. Airway support; naloxone (may not reverse seizures); benzodiazepines for seizures. Paracetamol (Acetaminophen): Potentially fatal hepatic necrosis; early symptoms may be absent. Give N-acetylcysteine as per nomogram – urgent treatment.
Evidence derives from component trials; multimodal analgesia principles support combining NSAID, paracetamol and weak opioid.
